title: Secular sabbath
hook: some people who keep no religion keep a weekly rest

segments.voice: Yesterday, the twelve steps, and a line people in recovery say to each other: one day at a time. Did today feel smaller, and more possible, held that way? Day one thousand four hundred twelve.

Saturday morning. The laptop is in a drawer. The phone is charging in another room, face down. There is no service to attend and no candle to light, because the person in this kitchen keeps no religion at all. And still, once a week, they stop. No email, no errands, no catching up. A long breakfast. A walk with no destination. A nap nobody earned. Ask them what they're doing and they might shrug and say, I'm keeping a sabbath, sort of. Some people who belong to no faith keep a weekly rest like this. The shape is borrowed. The question is what, exactly, they borrowed.
screen: `THE LAPTOP IN A DRAWER.` → `NO SERVICE, NO CANDLE.` → `A SABBATH, SORT OF.`

segments.voice: Start with where the word comes from. The sabbath is Jewish first, and it still belongs to the Jewish people, with its own laws and prayers and meaning. A secular sabbath borrows only its outline, and it should say so. Now look at that outline in the Torah itself. In Deuteronomy, the command is not only for you. Your children rest, your animals rest, the stranger in your town rests, and the text gives the reason plainly: "that thy manservant and thy maidservant may rest as well as thou." A day off that only the powerful get is not what the text describes. The rest is shared, or it isn't the thing. Then turn to the Gospel of Mark. Jesus is challenged about what may be done on the sabbath, and he answers, "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath." Christians and Jews read that line in their own ways. What a secular keeper takes from it is simpler: the day exists to serve a person, not to become one more task to perform well. Third turn: Thoreau, at Walden, wrote, "I love a broad margin to my life." A margin is the blank space around the writing on a page. Nothing is printed there, and without it, the page is a wall of text you can't read. So a secular sabbath has three borrowed parts. A regular time that comes back each week. A rest that includes the people around you. And a margin, where nothing has to be produced or proven.
screen: `JEWISH FIRST, AND STILL JEWISH.` · `REST THAT INCLUDES OTHERS.` · `MADE FOR THE PERSON, NOT THE TASK.` · `A BROAD MARGIN.` · then, large: `A REST DAY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one rest day. Settle, and let the breath slow. Look at the coming week. Find one day, or half a day if a whole one is impossible, that could be your margin. Ask three quiet questions. When will it start, and what small sign will mark it, a phone put away, a lamp turned off? Who else gets to rest because of it? And what one thing will you not do? Let the picture of that day become clear. The bell holds the time.
Secular sabbath. A weekly rest kept outside any religion, borrowing the shape of the Jewish sabbath: a regular time, a shared rest, a margin. Today's word.
Your line: a rest day. Today, put the day you chose into your calendar, and tell one person in your house when it is, so it can be theirs too. Day one thousand four hundred twelve.

howItsDone: People who keep a secular sabbath usually choose a regular weekly stretch, often a day or an evening, to set aside work, errands and screens, and spend it on meals, walks, rest and company; observant Jews keep Shabbat itself, with its own laws and prayers, from Friday sunset to Saturday night.

The script states plainly that the sabbath is Jewish first and still belongs to the Jewish people, and that the secular version borrows only its outline. A Jewish reader should confirm this framing is respectful.
Mark 2:27 is presented as a line Christians and Jews read in their own ways, with no claim about how. Confirm.
